common_name: Mathotiana Supreme Camellia (Large Ruffled Deep Red Sport of Mathotiana)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; a larger-flowered sport of the antique cultivar Mathotiana, one of the oldest camellias still grown in Southern gardens.

directions: Mathotiana Supreme is a sport of the nineteenth-century antique camellia Mathotiana, carrying the same deep, dark red color but on a larger, more heavily ruffled peony-to-rose form flower that opens over a long midseason display. The tall, upright, vigorous shrub eventually grows into a small tree with age, giving structure and glossy year-round foliage to a shaded border long before and after its winter bloom. Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to keep roots cool and evenly moist. Prune only lightly after bloom to shape, since camellias flower on the previous year's wood and heavy pruning sacrifices the coming season's buds.

common_name: Mathotiana Alba Camellia (White Formal Double Sport of Mathotiana)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; a white-flowered sport of the antique red cultivar Mathotiana, occasionally showing faint pink flecking within the same clump.

directions: Mathotiana Alba is a pure white, formal double sport of the deep red antique camellia Mathotiana, producing tightly imbricated, waxy-petaled flowers in midseason that show off well against the plant's dark, glossy evergreen foliage. Because sports of old camellia cultivars can occasionally revert or show streaked flowers on the same bush, it is not unusual to see a stray pink-flecked bloom appear among the white ones. The shrub shares its parent's tall, upright, slow-growing habit and eventually forms a substantial background specimen or small flowering tree in a shaded Southern garden. Grow in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, mulch to protect the shallow root system, and prune lightly right after flowering to maintain shape without removing next season's buds.

common_name: April Remembered Camellia (Cold-Hardy Pale Pink Ackerman Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; part of Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy camellia breeding line developed at the US National Arboretum for gardens colder than typical camellia country.

directions: April Remembered bears semi-double to peony-form flowers in a soft, pale pink that deepens slightly toward the petal base, blooming later in the season than most Ackerman-line camellias, which lets its buds dodge some of the hard freezes that can damage earlier-flowering cultivars. Like its siblings in the cold-hardy April series, it was bred by crossing Camellia japonica with the extremely hardy Camellia oleifera to extend camellia growing into regions well north of the plant's traditional Deep South range. The rounded, dense evergreen shrub works well as a foundation planting or informal hedge, holding glossy dark green foliage through winter even where flower buds occasionally freeze. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade and avoid harsh winter winds, which can desiccate foliage faster than cold alone.
sources: US National Arboretum — Ackerman Cold-Hardy Camellia Introductions

common_name: April Tryst Camellia (Cold-Hardy Deep Red Ackerman Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; one of the hardiest red-flowered cultivars in Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy April series of camellias.

directions: April Tryst produces deep red, semi-double flowers with a boss of gold stamens, standing out among the cold-hardy April series as one of the few reds bred to survive winters harsher than a traditional camellia range can tolerate. Its Camellia oleifera parentage gives the plant improved bud and wood hardiness compared with straight Camellia japonica cultivars, allowing gardeners well north of the Gulf Coast to grow a true camellia in the open border with minimal winter protection. The dense, rounded evergreen habit provides good year-round screening and looks equally at home as a specimen shrub or informal hedge. Site in moist, acidic, well-drained soil with afternoon shade, and mulch well to buffer root temperatures through cold snaps.
sources: US National Arboretum — Ackerman Cold-Hardy Camellia Introductions

common_name: Rev. John Bennett Camellia (Antique Red-and-White Striped Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; a nineteenth-century antique cultivar still grown for its bold red-and-white marbled petals.

directions: Rev. John Bennett is an antique camellia cultivar carried in old Southern gardens for its large, semi-double to loose peony-form flowers streaked and marbled in bold red and white, a striking pattern in the same family as better-known striped heirlooms like Tricolor and Governor Mouton. Individual flowers can vary from plant to plant and even bloom to bloom, part of the appeal for collectors of historic camellia cultivars. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub matures into a substantial specimen over many years, offering dense screening foliage in addition to its winter-to-spring flower display. Grow in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade, and mulch generously since old camellia cultivars are typically grafted or own-root plants with shallow, mulch-loving root systems.

common_name: Mrs. Charles Cobb Camellia (Dark Red Peony-Form Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; a long-cultivated, reliably vigorous dark red japonica popular for cut flowers as well as garden display.

directions: Mrs. Charles Cobb bears large, dark red, loose peony-form flowers with a subtle velvety sheen, opening over a long midseason-to-late bloom period on a vigorous, well-branched evergreen shrub. It has stayed in nursery and garden circulation for decades on the strength of its heavy, dependable flowering and its usefulness as a cut flower, since the sturdy petals hold up well once removed from the plant. The shrub's upright, dense habit makes it a good choice for a foundation planting, informal hedge, or shaded border backdrop where its glossy dark foliage provides interest well beyond the flowering season. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, water deeply during dry spells, and mulch to keep the root zone cool and evenly moist.

common_name: Frank Gauntlett Camellia (White Single Sasanqua with Pink Picotee Edge)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; sasanquas tolerate considerably more direct sun than Camellia japonica, making this a good choice for a sunnier Gulf Coast border.

directions: Frank Gauntlett produces single white flowers edged in a delicate pink picotee band, opening over a long fall bloom season on a dense, upright sasanqua shrub that takes pruning well and is often trained as a hedge or espalier against a wall. Like other sasanquas it flowers earlier in the year than Camellia japonica, providing color from autumn into early winter when little else is blooming in the Gulf Coast garden. Its greater sun tolerance compared with japonica types means it can go into a spot with several hours of direct sun without scorching, though afternoon shade in the hottest climates keeps flowers looking fresher longer. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil, mulch well, and shear lightly after bloom if a formal hedge shape is desired.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; a popular, compact landscape sasanqua for fall color in Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Bonanza bears semi-double to peony-form flowers in a warm red-orange that stands out against its dark, glossy foliage during the fall bloom season typical of sasanqua camellias. Its naturally compact, mounding habit is smaller and denser than many sasanquas, making it a practical choice for foundation plantings or a low informal hedge without constant shearing. Like other sasanquas, it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica and is a dependable performer through the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast growing season. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil, water regularly while establishing, and mulch to conserve moisture and protect the shallow root system through summer heat.

common_name: Glen 40 Camellia (Fred Sander, Formal Double Dark Red Exhibition Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; a long-standing exhibition-quality formal double favored for its perfectly imbricated petal arrangement.

directions: Glen 40, also sold and shown under the name Fred Sander, is an old formal double camellia bearing dark red flowers with tightly overlapping, symmetrically arranged petals that have made it a long-time favorite on the camellia show table. Bloom comes in midseason on a slow-growing but sturdy, dense, upright evergreen shrub that eventually becomes a substantial specimen with age. Because the flower form is so precise, growers wanting show-quality blooms often disbud to leave one flower per shoot, though the plant blooms heavily and attractively even left alone in an ordinary garden setting. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, mulch well, and avoid overhead watering that can spot the delicate formal double petals.

common_name: Grand Prix Camellia (Giant Rose-Red Semi-Double Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; a Nuccio's Nurseries introduction bred for exceptionally large exhibition-size blooms.

directions: Grand Prix produces some of the largest flowers in the camellia world, wide-open, semi-double, rose-red blooms centered with a prominent boss of golden stamens that give the flower a bold, dramatic presence against its dark evergreen foliage. Bred by Nuccio's Nurseries in California, it has become a favorite among camellia show exhibitors for its sheer flower size as well as a striking landscape specimen for gardeners who want an eye-catching midseason display. The upright, vigorous shrub needs a little more room than average to show off its outsized blooms without crowding. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through summer heat.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; one of the most widely planted fall-blooming camellias in the Gulf South for its spreading, sun-tolerant habit.

directions: Show-A-No-Sakae bears semi-double, blush-pink flowers with deeper pink veining and a ruffled edge, produced abundantly over a long fall-to-early-winter season on a naturally wide-spreading, somewhat sprawling shrub. Classed with the Camellia hiemalis group that sits between true sasanquas and japonicas, it shares the sasanqua group's tolerance for more direct sun and its fast, easy growth, making it a common choice for banks, large-scale groundcover plantings, and informal hedges across the Gulf South. Its spreading habit can be encouraged with light structural pruning when young or left to sprawl naturally as an informal mass planting. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil, water during dry spells while establishing, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat.

common_name: Kingyo-Tsubaki Camellia (Goldfish Camellia with Forked Fishtail Leaves)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; a curiosity cultivar grown chiefly for its unusual split, notched foliage rather than for its flower.

directions: Kingyo-Tsubaki, meaning "goldfish camellia" in Japanese, is grown mainly as a foliage curiosity rather than a flower specimen, since its glossy leaves end in an unusual forked, three- to five-lobed tip that resembles a goldfish's tail fin, a genetic quirk that breeds true in this old Japanese cultivar. It does still produce single to semi-double red flowers typical of Camellia japonica in season, but collectors and Japanese-garden enthusiasts prize it chiefly for the conversation-starting foliage that stays interesting year-round on the evergreen shrub. Give it the same care as any camellia: moist, humus-rich, acidic soil, partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun, and a generous organic mulch layer to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist. It makes an especially good container specimen near a patio or entry where the odd leaf shape can be appreciated up close.
